claim: During the rubber hand illusion (RHI), subjects experience an artificial hand as part of their own body.
source: During the rubber hand illusion (RHI), subjects experience an artificial hand as part of their own body, while the real hand is subject to a sort of 'disembodiment'.
evidence: This is a well-established phenomenon in the RHI literature, supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: During the RHI, the real hand is subject to a sort of 'disembodiment'.
source: During the rubber hand illusion (RHI), subjects experience an artificial hand as part of their own body, while the real hand is subject to a sort of 'disembodiment'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Ehrsson et al., 2004) and behavioral studies (Longo et al., 2008).

claim: The amplitude of motor-evoked potentials recorded from the real hand is significantly reduced with respect to baseline when subjects in the synchronous condition experience the fake hand as their own.
source: Our results show that the amplitude of the motor-evoked potentials recorded from the real hand is significantly reduced, with respect to baseline, when subjects in the synchronous (but not in the asynchronous) condition experience the fake hand as their own.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding supported by MEP measurements and statistical analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: The amplitude of motor-evoked potentials recorded from the real hand is not significantly reduced in the asynchronous condition.
source: Our results show that the amplitude of the motor-evoked potentials recorded from the real hand is significantly reduced, with respect to baseline, when subjects in the synchronous (but not in the asynchronous) condition experience the fake hand as their own.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing no significant difference between asynchronous and baseline conditions.

claim: A significant drop in motor excitability in M1 hand circuits accompanies the disembodiment of the real hand during the RHI experience.
source: This finding contributes to the theoretical understanding of the relationship between body-ownership and motor system, and provides the first physiological evidence that a significant drop in motor excitability in M1 hand circuits accompanies the disembodiment of the real hand during the RHI experience.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental MEP data.

claim: The sense of body ownership is the belief that a specific body part belongs to one's own body.
source: The sense of body ownership (i.e. the belief that a specific body part belongs to one's own body) (Gallagher, 2000) is a fundamental aspect of self-consciousness.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Gallagher, 2000.

claim: The sense of body ownership is a fundamental aspect of self-consciousness.
source: The sense of body ownership (i.e. the belief that a specific body part belongs to one's own body) (Gallagher, 2000) is a fundamental aspect of self-consciousness.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature (Gallagher, 2000).

claim: Body ownership as we normally experience it is the product of many different and complex operations.
source: However, both pathological cases after brain damage (somatoparaphrenia [Romano et al., 2014] and pathological embodiment [Pia et al., 2016; Fossataro et al., 2016; Garbarini et al., 2013, 2014, 2015; Pia et al., 2013; Garbarini and Pia, 2013]) and experimental manipulations in healthy subjects (e.g. the rubber hand illusion – RHI [Botvinick and Cohen, 1998]) suggest that body ownership, as we normally experience it, is the product of many different and complex operations.
evidence: This is inferred from pathological cases and experimental manipulations, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The feeling that our body belongs to us presumably depends on multisensory integration processes arising within a fronto-parietal network.
source: It has been suggested that the feeling that our body belongs to us presumably depends on multisensory integration processes arising within a fronto-parietal network, where sensory inputs coming from different modalities are realigned in a unique reference frame (Blanke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blanke et al., 2015.

claim: The ventral premotor cortex plays a crucial role in body ownership.
source: Within this network, the ventral premotor cortex seems to play a crucial role, thus establishing, both in monkeys (Graziano, 1999) and in humans (Makin et al., 2008; Ehrsson et al., 2004), an anatomical link between the sense of body ownership and the motor system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in monkeys (Graziano, 1999) and humans (Makin et al., 2008; Ehrsson et al., 2004).

claim: The ventral premotor cortex establishes an anatomical link between the sense of body ownership and the motor system in both monkeys and humans.
source: Within this network, the ventral premotor cortex seems to play a crucial role, thus establishing, both in monkeys (Graziano, 1999) and in humans (Makin et al., 2008; Ehrsson et al., 2004), an anatomical link between the sense of body ownership and the motor system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies (Graziano, 1999; Makin et al., 2008; Ehrsson et al., 2004).

claim: Voluntary motor activity of body parts contributes critically to the subjective experience of body ownership.
source: Furthermore, it has been proposed that voluntary motor activity of body parts contributes critically to the subjective experience of body ownership (Tsakiris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsakiris et al., 2010.

claim: During the RHI, the subject's hand-centered reference frame shifts towards the rubber hand.
source: During the illusion, the subject's hand-centered reference frame shifts towards the RH, and so it has been proposed that, as a consequence, the real hand is subject to a sort of disembodiment (Ehrsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ehrsson et al., 2004.

claim: A feeling of disownership of one's own hand has been reported as an important behavioural component of the RHI.
source: Accordingly, a feeling of disownership of one's own hand has been reported as an important behavioural component of the RHI (Longo et al., 2008), while a decrease in the temperature of the real (disembodied) hand has been observed as a neurophysiological correlate of the RHI (Moseley et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Longo et al., 2008.

claim: A decrease in the temperature of the real (disembodied) hand has been observed as a neurophysiological correlate of the RHI.
source: Accordingly, a feeling of disownership of one's own hand has been reported as an important behavioural component of the RHI (Longo et al., 2008), while a decrease in the temperature of the real (disembodied) hand has been observed as a neurophysiological correlate of the RHI (Moseley et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moseley et al., 2008.

claim: Cooling the subject's hand increases the strength of the RHI.
source: Moreover, it has been demonstrated that cooling the subject's hand increases the strength of the RHI, whereas warming the hand decreases it (Kammers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kammers et al., 2011.

claim: Warming the subject's hand decreases the strength of the RHI.
source: Moreover, it has been demonstrated that cooling the subject's hand increases the strength of the RHI, whereas warming the hand decreases it (Kammers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kammers et al., 2011.

claim: Hand-cooling can be present in both the experimental (synchronous) and the control (asynchronous) condition.
source: However, another study found that hand-cooling can be present in both the experimental (synchronous) and the control (asynchronous) condition, thus suggesting that it is not a reliable correlate of the subjective feeling of hand disownership in the RHI (Rohde et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rohde et al., 2013.

claim: Hand-cooling is not a reliable correlate of the subjective feeling of hand disownership in the RHI.
source: However, another study found that hand-cooling can be present in both the experimental (synchronous) and the control (asynchronous) condition, thus suggesting that it is not a reliable correlate of the subjective feeling of hand disownership in the RHI (Rohde et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of Rohde et al., 2013.

claim: Somatosensory changes observed in the participants' hand while experiencing the RHI can be explained by cross-modal mismatch between the seen and felt position of the hand.
source: A further study proposed that somatosensory changes observed in the participants' hand while experiencing the RHI can be explained by cross-modal mismatch between the seen and felt position of the hand, and are not necessarily a signature of disownership (Folegatti et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Folegatti et al., 2009.

claim: Somatosensory changes during RHI are not necessarily a signature of disownership.
source: A further study proposed that somatosensory changes observed in the participants' hand while experiencing the RHI can be explained by cross-modal mismatch between the seen and felt position of the hand, and are not necessarily a signature of disownership (Folegatti et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Folegatti et al., 2009.

claim: Proprioceptive drift towards the rubber hand was significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (4.51 ± 4.2 cm vs. 2.08 ± 2.75 cm; t(23)=2.783, p=0.0105, dz=0.58).
source: The main behavioral results showed that both proprioceptive drift towards the RH and embodiment questionnaire rating (emb-q-rating) were significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (drift=mean ± sd: 4.51 ± 4.2 cm vs. 2.08 ± 2.75 cm; t(23)=2.783, p=0.0105, dz=0.58; emb-q-rating=mean ± sd: 2.4 ± 0.64 vs. −2 ± 0.9, Z=4.2857, p=0.000018, dz=3.88; Figure 2A1 and A2; see also Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A1.

claim: Embodiment questionnaire rating was significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (2.4 ± 0.64 vs. −2 ± 0.9, Z=4.2857, p=0.000018, dz=3.88).
source: The main behavioral results showed that both proprioceptive drift towards the RH and embodiment questionnaire rating (emb-q-rating) were significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (drift=mean ± sd: 4.51 ± 4.2 cm vs. 2.08 ± 2.75 cm; t(23)=2.783, p=0.0105, dz=0.58; emb-q-rating=mean ± sd: 2.4 ± 0.64 vs. −2 ± 0.9, Z=4.2857, p=0.000018, dz=3.88; Figure 2A1 and A2; see also Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A2.

claim: No significant correlation was found between emb-q-rating and proprioceptive drift in the main behavioral experiment.
source: No significant correlation was found between emb-q-rating and proprioceptive drift.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: In the control behavioral experiment, proprioceptive drift was significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (2.47 ± 2.707 cm vs. 0.075 ± 2.461 cm; t(19)=5.275, p=0.000043, dz=1.18).
source: In the control behavioral experiment, similar results were found for both proprioceptive drift and emb-q-rating (drift=mean ± sd: 2.47 ± 2.707 cm vs. 0.075 ± 2.461 cm; t(19)=5.275, p=0.000043, dz=1.18; emb-q-rating=mean ± sd: 2 ± 0.763 vs. −0.97 ± 1.387; t(19)=9.357, p=0.0000001, dz=-2.1; Figure 2,B1 and B2; see also Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B1.

claim: In the control behavioral experiment, emb-q-rating was significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (2 ± 0.763 vs. −0.97 ± 1.387; t(19)=9.357, p=0.0000001, dz=-2.1).
source: In the control behavioral experiment, similar results were found for both proprioceptive drift and emb-q-rating (drift=mean ± sd: 2.47 ± 2.707 cm vs. 0.075 ± 2.461 cm; t(19)=5.275, p=0.000043, dz=1.18; emb-q-rating=mean ± sd: 2 ± 0.763 vs. −0.97 ± 1.387; t(19)=9.357, p=0.0000001, dz=-2.1; Figure 2,B1 and B2; see also Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B2.

claim: The disembodiment questionnaire rating was significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (0.153 ± 1.427 vs. −1.15 ± 1.371; t(19)=3.835, p=0.00116, dz==0.86).
source: Furthermore, the disembodiment questionnaire rating (disemb-q-rating) was significantly higher in the synchronous than in the asynchronous condition (disemb-q-rating=mean ± sd: 0.153 ± 1.427 vs. −1.15 ± 1.371; t(19)=3.835, p=0.00116, dz==0.86; Figure 2,B3; see also Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B3.

claim: Significant correlations were found between emb-q-rating and disemb-q-rating in both synchronous and asynchronous conditions and in the delta synchronous minus asynchronous (respectively: r-=-0.4911, p=0.0279; r-=-0.7128, p=0.0004; r-=-0.5537, p=0.0113).
source: Finally, significant correlations were found between emb-q-rating and disemb-q-rating in both synchronous and asynchronous conditions and in the delta synchronous minus asynchronous (respectively: r-=-0.4911, p=0.0279; r-=-0.7128, p=0.0004; r-=-0.5537, p=0.0113; Figure 2,C1,C2,C3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis and shown in Figure 2C1, C2, C3.

claim: No significant correlations were found between proprioceptive drift and either emb-q-rating or disemb-q-rating in the control behavioral experiment.
source: No significant correlations was found between proprioceptive drift and either emb-q-rating or disemb-q-rating.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The Friedman non-parametric ANOVA showed a significant effect of condition (χ2 [2, n=24]=9,000,000; p= 0.01111) for MEPs recorded from the stimulated (right) hand.
source: For the physiological data, the Friedman non-parametric ANOVA showed a significant effect of condition (χ2 [2, n=24]=9,000,000; p= 0.01111), suggesting a difference between baseline, synchronous and asynchronous conditions, when MEPs were recorded from the stimulated (right) hand.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the physiological data.

claim: There is a significant MEP decrease in the synchronous condition with respect to the asynchronous condition (−0.367 ± 0.362 vs. 0.205 ± 0.395; Z=3.3143, p=0.000919; dz=0.85).
source: Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, after Bonferroni correction, revealed a significant MEP decrease in the synchronous condition with respect to both the asynchronous (mean ± sd: −0.367 ± 0.362 vs. 0.205 ± 0.395; Z=3.3143, p=0.000919; dz=0.85) and the baseline (mean ± sd: −0.367 ± 0.362 vs. 0.277 ± 0.691; Z=3 .1428, p=0.001673; dz=0.74) conditions (Figure 3A1; see also Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of MEP data and shown in Figure 3A1.

claim: There is a significant MEP decrease in the synchronous condition with respect to the baseline condition (−0.367 ± 0.362 vs. 0.277 ± 0.691; Z=3.1428, p=0.001673; dz=0.74).
source: Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, after Bonferroni correction, revealed a significant MEP decrease in the synchronous condition with respect to both the asynchronous (mean ± sd: −0.367 ± 0.362 vs. 0.205 ± 0.395; Z=3.3143, p=0.000919; dz=0.85) and the baseline (mean ± sd: −0.367 ± 0.362 vs. 0.277 ± 0.691; Z=3 .1428, p=0.001673; dz=0.74) conditions (Figure 3A1; see also Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of MEP data and shown in Figure 3A1.

claim: No significant difference was found between asynchronous and baseline conditions (0.205 ± 0.395 vs. 0.277 ± 0.691; Z=0.1714, p=0.863887; dz=0.08).
source: No significant difference was found between asynchronous and baseline conditions (0.205 ± 0.395 vs. 0.277 ± 0.691; Z=0.1714, p=0.863887; dz=0.08).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of MEP data.

claim: The inhibitory motor response increases over time, with lower values measured at each time-point.
source: Interestingly, the MEP time-course analysis showed that the inhibitory motor response increases over time, with lower values measured at each time-point.
evidence: This is supported by time-course analysis of MEP data.

claim: There is a significant difference between TIME 1 (first five trials) and TIME 4 (last five trials) (−0.23963 ± 0.425821 vs. −0.5481 ± 0.394248; Z=2.942857; p=0.003252; dz=0.72).
source: Note that Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, after Bonferroni correction, showed a significant difference between TIME 1 (first five trials) and TIME 4 (last five trials) (mean ± sd: −0.23963 ± 0.425821 vs. −0.5481 ± 0.394248; Z=2.942857; p=0.003252; dz=0.72), Figure 3A2; see also Figure 3—source data 1.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of time-course MEP data and shown in Figure 3A2.

claim: In the control physiological experiment, no significant effect of condition was detected for the non-stimulated (left) hand (F(2,38)=0,894943; p=0.417068).
source: By contrast, in the control physiological experiment, in the three-level one-way ANOVA, no significant effect of condition was detected (F(2,38)=0,894943; p=0.417068), suggesting that for the non-stimulated (left) hand there is no difference between the synchronous condition and either the asynchronous (mean ± sd: −0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.045 ± 0.262; p=0.820737; dz=0.26) or baseline (mean ± sd: −0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.0572 ± 0.368; p=0.711483; dz=0.22) conditions (Figure 3B1; see also Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of MEP data for the control experiment, shown in Figure 3B1.

claim: For the non-stimulated (left) hand, there is no difference between the synchronous condition and the asynchronous condition (−0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.045 ± 0.262; p=0.820737; dz=0.26).
source: By contrast, in the control physiological experiment, in the three-level one-way ANOVA, no significant effect of condition was detected (F(2,38)=0,894943; p=0.417068), suggesting that for the non-stimulated (left) hand there is no difference between the synchronous condition and either the asynchronous (mean ± sd: −0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.045 ± 0.262; p=0.820737; dz=0.26) or baseline (mean ± sd: −0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.0572 ± 0.368; p=0.711483; dz=0.22) conditions (Figure 3B1; see also Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of MEP data for the control experiment, shown in Figure 3B1.

claim: For the non-stimulated (left) hand, there is no difference between the synchronous condition and the baseline condition (−0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.0572 ± 0.368; p=0.711483; dz=0.22).
source: By contrast, in the control physiological experiment, in the three-level one-way ANOVA, no significant effect of condition was detected (F(2,38)=0,894943; p=0.417068), suggesting that for the non-stimulated (left) hand there is no difference between the synchronous condition and either the asynchronous (mean ± sd: −0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.045 ± 0.262; p=0.820737; dz=0.26) or baseline (mean ± sd: −0.104 ± 0.399 vs. 0.0572 ± 0.368; p=0.711483; dz=0.22) conditions (Figure 3B1; see also Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of MEP data for the control experiment, shown in Figure 3B1.

claim: In the non-stimulated (left) hand, no significant effect of TIME was found (F(3,57)=0,842673; p=0.476191).
source: Moreover, in the four-level one-way ANOVA adopted for analysis of MEP time-course, no significant effect of TIME was found (F(3,57)=0,842673; p=0.476191), suggesting that in the non-stimulated (left) hand, MEP amplitude is not modulated over time (Figure 3B2; see also Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the time-course analysis of MEP data for the control experiment, shown in Figure 3B2.

claim: In the non-stimulated (left) hand, MEP amplitude is not modulated over time.
source: Moreover, in the four-level one-way ANOVA adopted for analysis of MEP time-course, no significant effect of TIME was found (F(3,57)=0,842673; p=0.476191), suggesting that in the non-stimulated (left) hand, MEP amplitude is not modulated over time (Figure 3B2; see also Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the negative finding of the time-course analysis, shown in Figure 3B2.

claim: There is a significant difference between the delta synchronous minus asynchronous obtained in the main experiment compared to the control experiment (−390.746 ± 591.662 vs. − 49.0296 ± 238.332; Z=2.074180; p=0.038063).
source: Additionally, the Mann-Whitney U-test revealed a significant difference between the delta synchronous minus asynchronous obtained in each experiment, showing a strong physiological effect of the RHI in the main compared to the control experiment (mean ± sd: −390.746 ± 591.662 vs. − 49.0296 ± 238.332; Z=2.074180; p=0.038063).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison between the two experiments.

claim: There is a strong physiological effect of the RHI in the main experiment compared to the control experiment.
source: Additionally, the Mann-Whitney U-test revealed a significant difference between the delta synchronous minus asynchronous obtained in each experiment, showing a strong physiological effect of the RHI in the main compared to the control experiment (mean ± sd: −390.746 ± 591.662 vs. − 49.0296 ± 238.332; Z=2.074180; p=0.038063).
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical comparison showing a significant difference between experiments.

claim: Voluntary movement of the real hand decreases the perceptual shift towards the rubber hand.
source: Recently, using a moving version of the RHI, it has been shown that voluntary (but not passive) movement of the real hand decreases the perceptual shift towards the rubber hand, suggesting that the subjective sense of agency strongly contributes to a coherent sense of body ownership (Tsakiris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsakiris et al., 2010.

claim: Passive movement of the real hand does not decrease the perceptual shift towards the rubber hand.
source: Recently, using a moving version of the RHI, it has been shown that voluntary (but not passive) movement of the real hand decreases the perceptual shift towards the rubber hand, suggesting that the subjective sense of agency strongly contributes to a coherent sense of body ownership (Tsakiris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsakiris et al., 2010.

claim: The subjective sense of agency strongly contributes to a coherent sense of body ownership.
source: Recently, using a moving version of the RHI, it has been shown that voluntary (but not passive) movement of the real hand decreases the perceptual shift towards the rubber hand, suggesting that the subjective sense of agency strongly contributes to a coherent sense of body ownership (Tsakiris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings cited from Tsakiris et al., 2010.

claim: Patients with schizophrenia show a specific deficit in predicting the consequences of their voluntary actions.
source: On the other hand, patients with schizophrenia, who show a specific deficit in predicting the consequences of their voluntary actions (Voss et al., 2010), as well as an altered sense of agency (Garbarini et al., 2016; Daprati et al., 1997; Maeda et al., 2012), are more susceptible to the RHI (Peled et al., 2003; Asai et al., 2011; Thakkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voss et al., 2010.

claim: Patients with schizophrenia show an altered sense of agency.
source: On the other hand, patients with schizophrenia, who show a specific deficit in predicting the consequences of their voluntary actions (Voss et al., 2010), as well as an altered sense of agency (Garbarini et al., 2016; Daprati et al., 1997; Maeda et al., 2012), are more susceptible to the RHI (Peled et al., 2003; Asai et al., 2011; Thakkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garbarini et al., 2016; Daprati et al., 1997; Maeda et al., 2012.

claim: Patients with schizophrenia are more susceptible to the RHI.
source: On the other hand, patients with schizophrenia, who show a specific deficit in predicting the consequences of their voluntary actions (Voss et al., 2010), as well as an altered sense of agency (Garbarini et al., 2016; Daprati et al., 1997; Maeda et al., 2012), are more susceptible to the RHI (Peled et al., 2003; Asai et al., 2011; Thakkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peled et al., 2003; Asai et al., 2011; Thakkar et al., 2011.

claim: Patients with focal hand dystonia seem to have some impairment of body ownership according to their susceptibility to the RHI paradigm.
source: Other studies on clinical populations with movement disorders suggest that patients with focal hand dystonia (Fiorio et al., 2011) or partial or complete paralysis because of spinal cord injury (Scandola et al., 2014; Tidoni et al., 2014) seem to have some impairment of body ownership, according to their susceptibility to the RHI paradigm.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fiorio et al., 2011.

claim: Patients with partial or complete paralysis because of spinal cord injury seem to have some impairment of body ownership according to their susceptibility to the RHI paradigm.
source: Other studies on clinical populations with movement disorders suggest that patients with focal hand dystonia (Fiorio et al., 2011) or partial or complete paralysis because of spinal cord injury (Scandola et al., 2014; Tidoni et al., 2014) seem to have some impairment of body ownership, according to their susceptibility to the RHI paradigm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scandola et al., 2014; Tidoni et al., 2014.

claim: Hemiplegic patients display a weaker/more flexible sense of body ownership for the affected (paralyzed) hand where the strength of the RHI is increased when compared to controls.
source: A recent study (Burin et al., 2015), investigating the RHI in movement disorder after brain-damage, shows that hemiplegic patients display a weaker/more flexible sense of body ownership for the affected (paralyzed) hand (where the strength of the RHI is increased) when compared to controls, but an enhanced/more rigid sense of body ownership for the healthy hand (where the strength of the RHI is decreased).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burin et al., 2015.

claim: Hemiplegic patients display an enhanced/more rigid sense of body ownership for the healthy hand where the strength of the RHI is decreased.
source: A recent study (Burin et al., 2015), investigating the RHI in movement disorder after brain-damage, shows that hemiplegic patients display a weaker/more flexible sense of body ownership for the affected (paralyzed) hand (where the strength of the RHI is increased) when compared to controls, but an enhanced/more rigid sense of body ownership for the healthy hand (where the strength of the RHI is decreased).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burin et al., 2015.

claim: The prolonged absence of movement makes the paralyzed limb more readily disowned.
source: In other words, the prolonged absence of movement makes the paralyzed limb more readily disowned, while the healthy limb seems to be more strongly owned.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of Burin et al., 2015.

claim: The healthy limb seems to be more strongly owned in hemiplegic patients.
source: In other words, the prolonged absence of movement makes the paralyzed limb more readily disowned, while the healthy limb seems to be more strongly owned.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of Burin et al., 2015.

claim: Healthy people can experience a pseudo-amputation illusion during a virtual reality procedure.
source: Kilteni and colleagues (2016) found that healthy people can experience a pseudo-amputation illusion during a virtual reality procedure, suggesting that this experimental manipulation causes corticospinal excitability changes in muscles associated with the virtually amputated body-part.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kilteni et al., 2016.

claim: A pseudo-amputation illusion causes corticospinal excitability changes in muscles associated with the virtually amputated body-part.
source: Kilteni and colleagues (2016) found that healthy people can experience a pseudo-amputation illusion during a virtual reality procedure, suggesting that this experimental manipulation causes corticospinal excitability changes in muscles associated with the virtually amputated body-part.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of Kilteni et al., 2016.

claim: After asynchronous stimulation, observing others' actions facilitated the motor system.
source: Schütz-Bosbach and colleagues (2006) studied how an action observation task can induce different changes in corticospinal excitability, depending on the level of ownership experienced with respect to the observed moving hand. Ownership was previously manipulated using the RHI procedure: after asynchronous stimulation, observing others' actions facilitated the motor system, whereas after synchronous stimulation, identical observed actions, now illusorily attributed to the subject's own body, evoked smaller MEPs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schütz-Bosbach et al., 2006.

claim: After synchronous stimulation, identical observed actions, now illusorily attributed to the subject's own body, evoked smaller MEPs.
source: Schütz-Bosbach and colleagues (2006) studied how an action observation task can induce different changes in corticospinal excitability, depending on the level of ownership experienced with respect to the observed moving hand. Ownership was previously manipulated using the RHI procedure: after asynchronous stimulation, observing others' actions facilitated the motor system, whereas after synchronous stimulation, identical observed actions, now illusorily attributed to the subject's own body, evoked smaller MEPs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schütz-Bosbach et al., 2006.

claim: The absence of facilitatory effect during observation following synchronous stimulation can be interpreted as resulting from the decreased corticospinal excitability induced by the illusion.
source: In light of our findings, the absence of facilitatory effect during observation following synchronous stimulation can be interpreted as resulting from the decreased corticospinal excitability induced by the illusion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings in relation to Schütz-Bosbach et al., 2006.

claim: Body ownership and the motor system are mutually interactive and both contribute to the dynamic construction of bodily self-awareness in healthy and pathological brains.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that body ownership and the motor system are mutually interactive and both contribute to the dynamic construction of bodily self-awareness in healthy and pathological brains.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the synthesis of multiple cited studies and the current findings.

claim: An experimental manipulation of the sense of body ownership is accompanied by a coherent modulation of the motor system.
source: In the present study, we found that the excitability of motor pathways in response to stimulation of the real (disembodied) hand is significantly decreased (i.e., MEP amplitude was significantly reduced) when subjects experience the artificial hand as their own. This suggests that an experimental manipulation of the sense of body ownership is accompanied by a coherent modulation of the motor system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The present data do not allow us to address the question of whether subjects who experience a larger subjective illusion also show a larger decrease in MEPs.
source: However, as the experimental design was not suited to investigate correlations (see details in Material and methods), the present data do not allow us to address the question of whether subjects who experience a larger subjective illusion also show a larger decrease in MEPs.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the experimental design.

claim: Active movements integrate distinct body parts into a unitary body representation.
source: It has been suggested that active movements integrate distinct body parts into a unitary body representation (Tsakiris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsakiris et al., 2010.

claim: When the unified body representation is altered, as during the visual-tactile conflict induced by the illusion, the excitability of the primary motor cortex is also altered.
source: When this unified representation is altered, as during the visual-tactile conflict induced by the illusion, the excitability of the primary motor cortex is also altered, suggesting that the motor readiness of the real (disembodied) hand could also be reduced.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The motor readiness of the real (disembodied) hand could be reduced when the unified body representation is altered.
source: When this unified representation is altered, as during the visual-tactile conflict induced by the illusion, the excitability of the primary motor cortex is also altered, suggesting that the motor readiness of the real (disembodied) hand could also be reduced.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The excitability decrease in the primary motor cortex (M1) is ascribed to cortical inhibitory processes tied to the central processing of hand ownership.
source: We ascribe the excitability decrease in the primary motor cortex (M1) to cortical inhibitory processes tied to the central processing of hand ownership, possibly reaching M1 via inhibitory input from the premotor cortex (which is known to play a crucial role in the multisensory integration processes that give rise to the sense of body ownership) (Ehrsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference and speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation to Ehrsson et al., 2004.

claim: The excitability decrease in M1 possibly reaches M1 via inhibitory input from the premotor cortex.
source: We ascribe the excitability decrease in the primary motor cortex (M1) to cortical inhibitory processes tied to the central processing of hand ownership, possibly reaching M1 via inhibitory input from the premotor cortex (which is known to play a crucial role in the multisensory integration processes that give rise to the sense of body ownership) (Ehrsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors, supported by citation to Ehrsson et al., 2004.

claim: The premotor cortex is known to play a crucial role in the multisensory integration processes that give rise to the sense of body ownership.
source: We ascribe the excitability decrease in the primary motor cortex (M1) to cortical inhibitory processes tied to the central processing of hand ownership, possibly reaching M1 via inhibitory input from the premotor cortex (which is known to play a crucial role in the multisensory integration processes that give rise to the sense of body ownership) (Ehrsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ehrsson et al., 2004.

claim: Bodily self-consciousness strictly depends on the possibility of movement.
source: The present findings, which shed new light on our understanding of the different aspects that contribute to the formation of a coherent self-awareness, suggest that bodily self-consciousness strictly depends on the possibility of movement.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The bodily self is primarily and originally construed in terms of motor potentiality for actions.
source: The bodily self is primarily and originally construed in terms of motor potentiality for actions (Gallese and Sinigaglia, 2010) .
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gallese and Sinigaglia, 2010.

claim: If I believe that the hand is mine, then I must be ready to use it; if not, then the activity of the motor system is accordingly down-regulated.
source: If I believe that the hand is mine, then I must be ready to use it; if not, then the activity of the motor system is accordingly down-regulated.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference drawn from the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Twenty-six volunteers (ten male, mean age ± SD=24 ± 5 years) took part in the behavioral main experiment.
source: Twenty-six (ten male) volunteers took part in the behavioral main experiment (mean age ± SD=24 ± 5 years) (the sample size estimation was performed according to an a priori power analysis, see details in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: A different sample of 26 subjects (ten male, mean age ± SD=24 ± 4 years) were recruited for the behavioural control experiment.
source: Additionally, a different sample of 26 subjects (ten male) (mean age ± SD=24 ± 4 years) were recruited for the behavioural control experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the control experimental sample.

claim: 24 out of 26 subjects participated in the physiological main experiment.
source: According to this criterion, 24 out of 26 subjects participated in the physiological main experiment; 20 out of 26 subjects participated in the physiological control experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size for the physiological experiment.

claim: 20 out of 26 subjects participated in the physiological control experiment.
source: According to this criterion, 24 out of 26 subjects participated in the physiological main experiment; 20 out of 26 subjects participated in the physiological control experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size for the control physiological experiment.

claim: All participants were right-handed, as assessed with the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: All participants were right-handed, as assessed with the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, and were screened to exclude a family history of psychiatric, neurological or medical disease.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: Participants were screened to exclude a family history of psychiatric, neurological or medical disease.
source: All participants were right-handed, as assessed with the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, and were screened to exclude a family history of psychiatric, neurological or medical disease.
evidence: This is a description of participant screening criteria.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano and written informed consent was obtained from each subject in compliance with the rules of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from each subject in compliance with the rules of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano and written informed consent was obtained from each subject in compliance with the rules of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: The RHI was evoked by the synchronous stroking of the rubber hand and of the participant's own hidden hand.
source: In both main (Figure 1A) and control (Figure 1B) experiments, the RHI was evoked by the synchronous stroking of the rubber hand and of the participant's own hidden hand (the location of stroking on the two hands was carefully matched) using the traditional visual-tactile stimulation (Botvinick and Cohen, 1998).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure, supported by citation to Botvinick and Cohen, 1998, and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Asynchronous stroking of a participant own hand and the rubber hand was utilized as a control condition.
source: Asynchronous stroking of a participant own hand and the rubber hand was utilized as a control condition, in which strokes were delivered spatially and temporally out of phase between the two hands.
evidence: This is a description of the control condition.

claim: The distance between the index finger of the rubber hand and the participant's own right index finger was 20 cm.
source: The distance between the index finger of the rubber hand and the participant's own right index finger was 20 cm.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Behavioral and physiological experiments were done in separate sessions.
source: Behavioral and physiological experiments were done in separate sessions: recording of MEPs in the three experimental conditions required about 40 min, and inserting the hand-ownership evaluation questions would have prolonged the experiment beyond a reasonable and feasible time, increasing the probability that subjects move their head with respect to the coil or lose their concentration on the task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with justification.

claim: Recording of MEPs in the three experimental conditions required about 40 min.
source: Behavioral and physiological experiments were done in separate sessions: recording of MEPs in the three experimental conditions required about 40 min, and inserting the hand-ownership evaluation questions would have prolonged the experiment beyond a reasonable and feasible time, increasing the probability that subjects move their head with respect to the coil or lose their concentration on the task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental duration.

claim: MEPs were elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the hand area in the left M1 in the main experiment.
source: In the main experiment, MEPs were elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the hand area in the left M1 and recorded by self-adhesive bipolar surface electrodes that were placed over the belly of the right first dorsal interosseous muscle (FDI).
evidence: This is a description of the physiological measurement method.

claim: MEPs were recorded by self-adhesive bipolar surface electrodes placed over the belly of the right first dorsal interosseous muscle (FDI) in the main experiment.
source: In the main experiment, MEPs were elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the hand area in the left M1 and recorded by self-adhesive bipolar surface electrodes that were placed over the belly of the right first dorsal interosseous muscle (FDI).
evidence: This is a description of the recording method.

claim: The stimulator output was set at about 110% of each subject's motor threshold.
source: The coil was positioned and fixed on the left primary motor cortex with the handle pointing backwards at 45% from the midline so as to activate the selected muscle, and the stimulator output was set at about 110% of each subject's motor threshold (defined as the intensity giving three MEP responses out of six stimuli) (Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the TMS parameters, supported by citations to Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008.

claim: Motor threshold is defined as the intensity giving three MEP responses out of six stimuli.
source: The coil was positioned and fixed on the left primary motor cortex with the handle pointing backwards at 45% from the midline so as to activate the selected muscle, and the stimulator output was set at about 110% of each subject's motor threshold (defined as the intensity giving three MEP responses out of six stimuli) (Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008.

claim: In the control experiment, MEPs were elicited by single-pulse TMS of the hand area in the right M1 and recorded with self-adhesive bipolar surface electrodes over the left FDI belly.
source: We replicated the same procedure in the control experiment, but in this case, MEPs were elicited by single-pulse TMS of the hand area in the right M1 and recorded with self-adhesive bipolar surface electrodes over the left FDI belly.
evidence: This is a description of the control experiment procedure.

claim: At the beginning of each experiment, 20 MEPs were recorded without visual-tactile stimulation and taken as a measure of motor-cortex excitability in a neutral condition.
source: At the very beginning of each experiment, after they gave their informed consent, subjects were asked to watch a cross on a pc screen while sitting in a comfortable chair. In the meantime, 20 MEPs were recorded (without visual-tactile stimulation) and taken as a measure of motor-cortex excitability in a neutral condition.
evidence: This is a description of the baseline measurement procedure.

claim: Participants were asked to judge the perceived location of their unseen right index finger by verbally indicating a number on a ruler presented on top of the box in front of them.
source: In both main and control experiments, participants were asked to judge the perceived location of their unseen right index finger by verbally indicating a number on a ruler presented on top of the box in front of them.
evidence: This is a description of the proprioceptive drift measurement method.

claim: The difference between the indicated location of the participant's right index finger before and after the visual-tactile stimulation was taken as a measure of perceptual relocation.
source: The difference between the indicated location of the participant's right index finger before and after the visual-tactile stimulation was taken as a measure of perceptual relocation.
evidence: This is a description of how proprioceptive drift was calculated.

claim: An ownership questionnaire consisting of three statements was administered to evaluate the subjective experience of the RHI.
source: In order to evaluate the subjective experience of the RHI, an ownership questionnaire (emb-q-rating) consisting of three statements was administered; participants were asked to evaluate the vividness of their experience of ownership of the rubber hand using a 7 points Likert scale (–3=strong disagreement; +3=strong agreement; 0=neither agreement nor disagreement), with the following three items: "It seemed as if I were feeling the touch in the location where I saw the rubber hand touched", "It seemed as though the touch I felt was caused by the touch over the rubber hand", "I felt as if the rubber hand were my hand".
evidence: This is a description of the subjective measurement method.

claim: The ownership questionnaire statements were based on the traditional RHI study.
source: The statements were based on the traditional RHI study (Botvinick and Cohen, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Botvinick and Cohen, 1998.

claim: Subjects participated in the physiological experiments only if they gave a rating higher than zero in the synchronous condition in the embodiment questionnaire.
source: Subjects participated in the physiological experiments only if, in the embodiment questionnaire, they gave a rating higher than zero in the synchronous condition.
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criterion for the physiological experiment.

claim: Two subjects in the main experiment were not admitted to the physiological experiment according to the rating criterion.
source: Note that, according to this criterion, two subjects in the main experiment were not admitted to the physiological experiment.
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusion.

claim: A disownership questionnaire consisting of three statements was administered in the control experiment to verify whether the feeling of ownership of the RH is coherently accompanied by a feeling of disownership of the stimulated hand.
source: Moreover, in the control experiment, in order to verify whether the feeling of ownership of the RH is coherently accompanied by a feeling of disownership of the stimulated hand, a disownership questionnaire (disemb-q-rating) consisting of three statements was also administered.
evidence: This is a description of an additional measurement in the control experiment.

claim: The disownership questionnaire statements were selected from a study proposing a psychometric approach to body ownership.
source: The statements were selected from a study proposing a psychometric approach to body ownership (Longo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Longo et al., 2008.

claim: 20 MEPs were recorded during both synchronous and asynchronous conditions in the physiological experiments.
source: For both main and control experiments, at the end of the behavioral procedure, 20 MEPs were recorded during both synchronous and asynchronous conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the physiological data collection.

claim: The order of the experimental blocks (synchronous-asynchronous; asynchronous-synchronous) was counterbalanced between subjects.
source: The order of the experimental blocks (synchronous-asynchronous; asynchronous-synchronous) was counterbalanced between subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design to control for order effects.

claim: Each visual-tactile stimulation cycle lasted 12 s.
source: Each visual-tactile stimulation cycle lasted 12 s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timing.

claim: Two seconds after the end of each cycle, a single-pulse TMS was triggered to induce a MEP.
source: Two seconds after the end of each cycle, a single-pulse TMS was triggered to induce a MEP, using a custom-made synchronizing program in LabView10.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timing and procedure.

claim: For each subject, 60 MEPs were recorded: 20 during the baseline conditions and 40 during the visual-tactile stimulation (20 during the synchronous block; 20 during the asynchronous).
source: Therefore, for each subject, 60 MEPs were recorded: 20 during the baseline conditions (at the beginning of the whole procedure) and 40 during the visual-tactile stimulation (20 during the synchronous block; 20 during the asynchronous).
evidence: This is a description of the total number of measurements per subject.

claim: Participants were exposed to both experimental blocks (synchronous/asynchronous) in the same experimental session, with a resting break between the blocks lasting about 5 min.
source: Participants were exposed to both experimental blocks (synchronous/asynchronous) in the same experimental session, with a resting break between the blocks (lasting about 5 min).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental session structure.

claim: The return of cortical excitability to baseline level was always ascertained before starting each block of visuo-tactile stimulation.
source: The return of cortical excitability to baseline level was always ascertained before starting each block of visuo-tactile stimulation.
evidence: This is a description of a control procedure to ensure valid measurements.

claim: The whole experimental procedure, including behavioral and physiological experiment, lasted about 40 min.
source: The whole experimental procedure, including behavioral and physiological experiment, lasted about 40 min.
evidence: This is a description of the total experimental duration.

claim: MEP amplitude of the FDI muscle was measured as the peak-to-peak distance (in µV).
source: MEP amplitude of the FDI muscle was measured as the peak-to-peak distance (in µV), and MEPs of amplitude lower than 50 µV were discarded from analysis (Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the MEP measurement method, supported by citations.

claim: MEPs of amplitude lower than 50 µV were discarded from analysis.
source: MEP amplitude of the FDI muscle was measured as the peak-to-peak distance (in µV), and MEPs of amplitude lower than 50 µV were discarded from analysis (Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criterion, supported by citations to Rossini et al., 1994; Borroni et al., 2008.

claim: The present experimental design was not ideally suited to investigate correlations between behavioral and physiological data.
source: We acknowledge that the present experimental design was not ideally suited to investigate correlations, due to the fact that behavioural and physiological data were acquired in two separate sessions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the experimental design.

claim: Only responder subjects were admitted to the physiological experiment.
source: Furthermore, only responder subjects were admitted to the physiological experiment, i.e. we use only subjects who gave ratings higher than zero in the synchronous condition in the embodiment questionnaire administered during the behavioural experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the selection criterion for the physiological experiment.

claim: In the present sample, which only includes responder subjects, correlations between physiological parameters and the presence/absence of the illusion cannot be investigated.
source: Thus, in the present sample, which only includes responder subjects, correlations between physiological parameters and the presence/absence of the illusion cannot be investigated.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation resulting from the selection criterion.

claim: No significant correlations with MEPs were found for questionnaire ratings or for proprioceptive drift.
source: In both cases, we used two different approaches: a) we normalized MEP values, ratings and drift values by using z-scores to compute independent correlations for synchronous and asynchronous conditions: significant correlations with MEPs were not found, neither for questionnaire ratings nor for proprioceptive drift; b) for MEP values, ratings and drift values, we computed a delta (synchronous minus asynchronous) value and performed correlations on these values: again, no significant correlations with MEPs were found for questionnaire ratings or for proprioceptive drift.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the correlation analysis.
